passages.happening:
Hear what the LORD says. Plead the case before the mountains, and let the hills hear (verse 1). ‘Hear, O mountains, the LORD’s indictment, you enduring foundations of the earth. For the LORD has a case against His people’ (verse 2).

Then God speaks, and he does not list Israel's crimes. He asks a question. ‘My people, what have I done to you?’ (verse 3). How has he wearied them? ‘For I brought you up from the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery. I sent Moses before you, as well as Aaron and Miriam’ (verse 4). They should remember what Balak king of Moab planned and how Balaam answered him, and remember the way from Shittim to Gilgal, so that they know the LORD's saving acts (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The scene draws on the ancient courtroom and on treaty practice. When a king made a covenant with a lesser king, gods and forces of nature were often called as witnesses, and Israel's covenant texts call on heaven and earth. Here the mountains and the foundations of the earth are summoned to hear the LORD's case. The word for case, riv, is the ordinary word for a legal dispute, and scholars call passages like this a covenant lawsuit.

The plaintiff is the wounded party, and he speaks like a hurt parent, calling them his people twice. Instead of a list of charges, he recites what he has done. Balak king of Moab hired the seer Balaam to curse Israel, and God turned every curse around. Shittim was Israel's last camp east of the Jordan and Gilgal its first camp after crossing, so from Shittim to Gilgal recalls the entry into the land.
passages.later: Balaam was hired to curse Israel (Numbers 22 to 24), and Israel crossed the Jordan from Shittim to Gilgal (Joshua 3 to 4). Moses also called heaven and earth to listen: ‘Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak’ (Deuteronomy 32:1).
passages.asks: God answers his people's coldness by asking what he has done to them. Ask what you would say if he asked you. And ask what God has done in your own story that you have stopped remembering.

passages.happening:
A worshiper asks what he should bring. ‘With what shall I come before the LORD when I bow before the God on high? Should I come to Him with burnt offerings, with year-old calves?’ (verse 6). Would the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, with ten thousand rivers of oil? Should he even give his firstborn for his sin (verse 7)?

‘He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The worshiper's questions rise in four steps: year-old calves, thousands of rams, rivers of oil, a firstborn child. Each is bigger than the last. The worshiper is trying to find the price.

The question about a firstborn was not idle. Second Kings records that King Ahaz sacrificed his son, and his grandson Manasseh did the same. Child sacrifice was known among Israel's neighbors, and the law forbade it outright. These notes name it as the text does and do not describe it. God never asks it.

Verse 8 answers all four questions with three things. To act justly is mishpat, fair dealing and fair judgment. To love mercy is to love hesed, loyal, faithful love. To walk humbly with God is to live close to him, without pretending. The answer is not new: he has shown you. The God who asks it has already redeemed his people (verse 4).
passages.later: The law forbade giving a child in the fire (Leviticus 18:21). Samuel told Saul, ‘obedience is better than sacrifice’ (1 Samuel 15:22), and Hosea heard God say, ‘For I desire mercy, not sacrifice’ (Hosea 6:6).
passages.hard:
Does Micah 6:8 mean that God does not care about sacrifice and worship, only about how people behave?

Some modern readers have taken this verse as the prophets' rejection of ritual religion in favor of pure morality. Most interpreters think that reads too much into it. The prophets did attack worship that was cut off from justice, but they did not abolish the temple or its offerings, and Micah himself hopes for the nations streaming to the house of the LORD (4:1-2). The point of verses 6 to 8 is that no quantity of offerings can stand in for a life given to God, and that the worshiper's bargaining misunderstands who God is. Walking humbly with God includes worship. It refuses worship as a transaction.

Christians add that the sacrifices themselves pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering, which is why the church does not offer animal sacrifices, not because worship stopped mattering. And verse 8 is often quoted alone as a ladder to earn God's favor. In context it is the shape of life for a people God has already rescued.
passages.asks: The worshiper kept raising the price. Ask whether you have tried to make up to God with things, when he asked for your life. And ask which of the three, justice, mercy or humility, comes hardest to you.

passages.t: Short measures, and labor without fruit
passages.happening:
The voice of the LORD calls to the city, and it is wisdom to fear his name (verse 9). Can he forget the treasures gained by wickedness, ‘and the short ephah, which is accursed?’ (verse 10). ‘Can I excuse dishonest scales or bags of false weights?’ (verse 11). The city's wealthy are full of violence, and its people speak lies (verse 12).

So God is striking them (verse 13). ‘You will eat but not be satisfied’ (verse 14). What they save will not last. ‘You will sow but not reap; you will press olives but not anoint yourselves with oil; you will tread grapes but not drink the wine’ (verse 15). They have kept the statutes of Omri and all the practices of Ahab's house, so they will become a desolation and bear the scorn of the nations (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The chapter moves from the courtroom to the market. Grain was measured by the ephah, and silver was weighed on scales against stones kept in a bag. A short ephah or a light stone cheated the buyer, a sin the law named directly and Amos had condemned a generation earlier.

The punishment is a string of futility curses: every labor stops short of its fruit. They eat and stay hungry, sow and do not reap, press olives and grapes and never enjoy them.

Verse 16 reaches back to the ninth century, to Omri, who founded Samaria as the northern capital, and his son Ahab, whose reign with Jezebel became the Bible's byword for Baal worship and for the judicial murder of Naboth to take his vineyard. To say Jerusalem keeps the statutes of Omri is to say the southern capital has taken on the ways of the northern one God had just judged.
passages.later: The law forbade false measures (Deuteronomy 25:13-16), and Amos condemned merchants who made ‘the ephah’ small (Amos 8:5). Naboth's vineyard was taken by Ahab and Jezebel through a false trial (1 Kings 21).
passages.asks: The city's wealth was built on short measures, and none of it satisfied. Ask whether anything you have gained by cutting corners has given you rest. And ask what honest measure would look like in your own work.
